(CNN)  -- Two former presidents reflected on their greatest regrets in office Monday, each looking back to issues that continue to plague the nation years later. Former presidents and political rivals Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush now share philanthropic efforts. Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana. Asked his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to get Saddam Hussein to leave office at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991. He told the gathering, "I've thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table, surrendered. And the common wisdom was he wouldn't do that." But he said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after he was captured has made him reconsider. Bush recalled their talk, "I said, 'What if we just say he has to come to surrender, would he have done it?' And this guy said, 'I'm absolutely convinced he would have.' My experts tell me he wouldn't have." Bush said, "We ended it the way we said we would" as a military success, but noted a cleaner ending "would have been perfect." He added, "If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have been avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him." On a day that President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed the failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians. "My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted. "If he had done that ... we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel where not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over West Bank then than they do today," Clinton said. "And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state and we would have had, I think now, normal peaceful relations with Israel and all of its Arab neighbors." Clinton said a deal would have helped the U.S. handle other issues in the region, saying, "We'd be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one. And so, I think that would have done more good to save more lives and help more people, and I wish I had been able to do that. " Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to "stop the Rwandan genocide," and succeeding on a new health care plan. He said "presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made" with historians, because it teaches lessons. He said he shared problems during the lunch with Obama and the four living presidents, saying, "You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones." Clinton added, "all of us know if you make enough decisions, you're going to make a few of them aren't right."

outputs.L1:
(CNN) — Two former presidents reflected Monday on their greatest regrets in office, revisiting issues that continue to trouble the nation years later.

Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton—once political rivals who now collaborate on philanthropic efforts—appeared together at a question-and-answer forum before the National Automobile Dealers Association in New Orleans, Louisiana.

Asked about his biggest regret after leaving office, Bush said he now wonders whether he should have tried to persuade Saddam Hussein to surrender at the end of the first Gulf War in 1991.

“I’ve thought a lot about it, but at the end of Desert Storm, the question was: Should we have kind of kept going on that road to death and all this slaughter until Saddam Hussein showed up and laid his sword on the table—surrendered?” Bush told the gathering. “And the common wisdom was he wouldn’t do that.”

However, Bush said a conversation with an FBI agent who interrogated Saddam after his capture prompted him to reconsider.

Bush recalled their exchange: “I said, ‘What if we just say he has to come to surrender? Would he have done it?’ And this guy said, ‘I’m absolutely convinced he would have.’ My experts tell me he wouldn’t have.”

“We ended it the way we said we would,” Bush said, describing the operation as a military success, but noting that a cleaner conclusion “would have been perfect.”

“If we had tried to get Saddam Hussein to come and literally surrender and put his sword on the table, I think it might have avoided some of the problems that we did have in the future from him,” he added.

On a day when President Barack Obama dispatched George Mitchell to the Middle East as the latest U.S. envoy, Clinton discussed his failure to achieve peace between Israelis and Palestinians.

“My No. 1 regret is that I was not able to persuade Yasser Arafat to accept the peace plan I offered at the end of my presidency that the Israelis accepted,” Clinton said.

“If he had done that, we had had seven years of progress toward peace. We had one year, in 1998, the only year in the history of Israel when not a single soul was killed in a terrorist act. The Palestinians had more control over the West Bank then than they do today,” Clinton said.

“And if he had taken that deal, we would have a Palestinian state, and we would have had, I think by now, normal, peaceful relations between Israel and all of its Arab neighbors.”

Clinton said an agreement would also have helped the United States address other issues in the region.

“We’d be much better positioned to deal with the problem of Iran, and we would have taken away about half the arguments of terrorists around the world by giving the Palestinians their state and creating a cooperative, positive interdependence in the Middle East, not a negative one,” he said.

“And so, I think that would have done more good, saved more lives and helped more people, and I wish I had been able to do that.”

Clinton also said he regretted not doing more to “stop the Rwandan genocide” and not succeeding in enacting a new health care plan.

He said “presidents should share freely ... the mistakes they made” with historians because doing so provides valuable lessons. Clinton said he discussed such problems during a lunch with Obama and the four living presidents.

“You want each new president to make new mistakes, not the same ones,” he said.

Clinton added, “All of us know that if you make enough decisions, you’re going to make a few that aren’t right.”

(CNN) — During a Monday appearance, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton spoke about the decisions they most wished they could revisit—choices involving problems that still confront the United States years later.

Bush and Clinton, once political opponents, have since joined forces on charitable initiatives. The two appeared together in New Orleans, Louisiana, for a question-and-answer session hosted by the National Automobile Dealers Association.

When asked about his greatest post-presidential regret, Bush said he has questioned whether, at the conclusion of the 1991 Gulf War, he should have pushed Saddam Hussein to personally surrender and give up power.

Bush explained that when Operation Desert Storm ended, his administration had to decide whether to continue advancing, with the additional deaths and destruction that would have involved, until Saddam appeared and formally laid down his sword. At the time, advisers generally believed the Iraqi leader would never agree to such a surrender.

However, Bush said he later reconsidered after speaking with an FBI agent who questioned Saddam following his capture. According to Bush, he asked the agent whether Saddam would have surrendered if the United States had made that an explicit requirement. The agent replied that he was completely certain Saddam would have done so, contradicting the advice Bush had received from his own experts.

Bush emphasized that the military campaign concluded as the United States had promised and was successful. Still, he said the outcome would have been ideal if Saddam had been compelled to surrender in person. In Bush’s view, such an ending might have prevented some of the later difficulties caused by the Iraqi leader.

Clinton, meanwhile, addressed the unresolved Israeli-Palestinian conflict on the same day President Barack Obama sent George Mitchell to the Middle East as the newest American envoy to the region.

Clinton identified his foremost regret as his inability, near the end of his presidency, to convince Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to approve a peace proposal that Israel had already accepted.

He said the preceding seven years had produced movement toward peace. Clinton pointed to 1998 as the only year in Israel’s history in which terrorism did not claim a single life. He also noted that Palestinians then exercised greater authority over the West Bank than they do today.

Had Arafat accepted the proposal, Clinton said, a Palestinian nation would have been established and Israel probably would now have normal, peaceful ties with all neighboring Arab countries.

Clinton argued that an agreement also would have strengthened Washington’s ability to address other regional challenges, including Iran. He said the creation of a Palestinian state, along with constructive and mutually beneficial relationships in the Middle East, would have eliminated roughly half of the claims used by terrorists worldwide. In his assessment, achieving that outcome would have saved more lives and improved conditions for more people, and he wished he had succeeded.

Clinton named two other disappointments from his presidency: failing to take stronger action to prevent the genocide in Rwanda and not securing passage of a new health care plan.

He said former presidents should be candid with historians about their errors because future leaders can learn from them. Clinton added that, during a lunch attended by Obama and all four living former presidents, he discussed past difficulties. His view was that every incoming president should make different mistakes rather than repeat those of predecessors.

Clinton concluded that anyone who makes a large number of decisions will inevitably make some incorrect ones.

outputs.L4:
Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton reflected on the most painful foreign-policy disappointments of their administrations during a joint public forum, with both men focusing on decisions whose consequences continued to shape the Middle East long after they left office.

Bush looked back on the 1991 Gulf War, in which a U.S.-led coalition drove Iraqi forces out of Kuwait. Although the military campaign achieved its immediate objective, Saddam Hussein remained in power. Bush said he sometimes wondered whether the coalition should have required the Iraqi leader to surrender personally before ending the conflict. Such a demand, he suggested, might have weakened Saddam’s hold on Iraq or prevented some of the instability that followed. His remarks highlighted the enduring debate over whether the war stopped at the right moment and whether a different conclusion could have altered the region’s later history.

Clinton’s regret centered on the Israeli-Palestinian peace process. He recalled the extensive negotiations undertaken during his presidency and the effort to reach a comprehensive settlement near the end of his second term. Israel accepted the proposed framework, Clinton said, but Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat rejected it. Clinton indicated that the missed opportunity remained deeply troubling because he believed the plan could have moved both sides closer to ending decades of conflict.

The former presidents’ comments revealed how even policies considered successful at the time can leave lasting doubts. Bush’s coalition liberated Kuwait but did not remove Saddam, while Clinton helped bring Israeli and Palestinian leaders closer to an agreement without securing a final peace. In both cases, the unresolved outcomes continued to influence violence, instability and diplomacy across the Middle East.

Their reflections also underscored the limits of presidential power. Leaders can build coalitions, conduct wars and broker negotiations, but they cannot always control what allies, adversaries or future governments will do. For Bush and Clinton, the central questions were therefore not simply about what happened during their presidencies, but about whether different choices at decisive moments might have spared the region years of further turmoil.

counterfactuals.output:
# Clinton, elder Bush reflect on presidential regrets at New Orleans forum

**NEW ORLEANS (CNN)** — Former Presidents Bill Clinton and George H.W. Bush looked back on the most difficult moments of their administrations during an appearance before the National Automobile Dealers Association, offering candid reflections on war, genocide and the political costs of decisions made in the White House.

Clinton said his greatest regret was the failure of the United States and the international community to intervene during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda, in which an estimated 800,000 people were killed in about 100 days.

The former president said he has often wondered whether a modest international force could have saved hundreds of thousands of lives. Clinton later traveled to Rwanda and acknowledged that the world had not acted quickly enough to stop the slaughter.

Bush, the nation’s 41st president, was more reluctant to identify a single regret. He pointed to the political damage caused by breaking his 1988 campaign promise, “Read my lips: no new taxes,” after agreeing to a budget compromise that included tax increases.

The decision helped reduce the federal deficit but angered conservatives and became a major issue in Bush’s unsuccessful 1992 re-election campaign against Clinton.

Bush also reflected on the 1991 Persian Gulf War and defended his decision not to send U.S. forces to Baghdad after driving Iraqi troops out of Kuwait. Going beyond the United Nations mandate, he suggested, could have left American forces occupying Iraq without a clear exit strategy.

The conversation highlighted the friendship the two former political rivals developed after leaving office. Clinton defeated Bush in 1992, but the two later worked together on relief efforts following the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and Hurricane Katrina.

Their appearance in New Orleans mixed serious discussion with humor and friendly exchanges, drawing applause from automobile dealers gathered at a time of deep uncertainty for the industry.

Both men emphasized that presidential decisions are often made with incomplete information and carry consequences that may not become clear until years later.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the remarks made by former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton about Saddam Hussein, the Gulf War, Israeli-Palestinian peace, and Rwanda during their joint appearance Monday.
counterfactuals.output:
During their joint appearance Monday, former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton largely agreed on the historical issues they discussed:

- **Saddam Hussein:** Both described Saddam as a dangerous and brutal dictator. Bush said the world was better off without him, while avoiding detailed criticism of his son’s conduct of the Iraq war. Clinton likewise said Saddam’s removal was welcome, although that did not settle questions about how the 2003 war was undertaken or managed.

- **The 1991 Gulf War:** Bush defended his decision to stop after liberating Kuwait rather than send coalition forces to Baghdad. He said the U.N. mandate and coalition had been assembled for the limited purpose of expelling Iraq from Kuwait; occupying Iraq would have fractured that coalition and left the United States responsible for governing the country. Clinton supported Bush’s judgment and said he would have made essentially the same decision.

- **Israeli-Palestinian peace:** Clinton said the peace process came close to producing an agreement late in his presidency, but Yasser Arafat failed to accept the opportunity offered to him. He also emphasized the damage caused by Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin’s assassination. Bush pointed to the 1991 Madrid conference as an important step that helped make the later Oslo process possible.

- **Rwanda:** Clinton again called the failure to act more forcefully during the 1994 genocide one of the deepest regrets of his presidency. He said a relatively modest international military deployment might have saved large numbers of lives. Bush responded sympathetically, suggesting Clinton should not bear the burden alone for the international community’s failure.

The exchange was notably cordial: each man defended or praised important decisions made by the other despite their partisan differences.

## Bush, Clinton Cite Missed Chances With Saddam Hussein and Yasser Arafat Among Their Greatest Regrets

**WASHINGTON —** Former Presidents George H.W. Bush and Bill Clinton, reflecting on defining foreign-policy crises of their administrations, identified missed opportunities involving two of the Middle East’s most consequential leaders as major regrets of their presidencies.

In a question-and-answer session, Bush said he regretted not pressing for Iraqi President Saddam Hussein’s formal surrender after the U.S.-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait in 1991. Clinton, meanwhile, said he regretted being unable to persuade Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat to accept a peace agreement during the final stretch of his administration.

Their comments offered unusually direct assessments of decisions that shaped American involvement in the Middle East for decades. In both cases, the former presidents described moments of overwhelming American diplomatic or military influence that nevertheless failed to produce lasting political settlements.

Bush’s regret centers on the conclusion of the Persian Gulf War, when a coalition led by the United States drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait after a six-week air campaign and a ground offensive lasting roughly 100 hours. Bush halted the advance after the coalition had achieved the United Nations-backed objective of liberating Kuwait.

Iraqi military representatives subsequently accepted cease-fire terms, but Saddam remained in power in Baghdad. The coalition did not demand his personal surrender or attempt to remove his government.

Bush and his senior advisers long defended that decision, arguing that pushing farther into Iraq would have exceeded the coalition’s mandate, fractured international support and drawn American forces into an open-ended occupation. In the Q&A, however, Bush suggested that the failure to seek Saddam’s surrender left the war without the kind of decisive political conclusion that might have constrained the Iraqi ruler more effectively.

The aftermath was turbulent. Shiite and Kurdish uprisings erupted in Iraq, only to be violently suppressed by Saddam’s forces. The United States and its allies established no-fly zones, maintained sanctions and repeatedly confronted Iraq over weapons inspections. Saddam remained in power until the 2003 U.S.-led invasion ordered by Bush’s son, President George W. Bush.

The elder Bush’s reflection does not necessarily amount to an endorsement of occupying Baghdad or overthrowing the Iraqi government in 1991. A demand for surrender could have taken several forms, including stronger political terms or a public acknowledgment of defeat by Saddam. Still, the comment points to a persistent question surrounding the first Gulf War: whether its limited military objective produced an incomplete strategic result.

Clinton’s regret focused on a different kind of unfinished campaign — his administration’s effort to broker a comprehensive agreement between Israel and the Palestinians.

Clinton invested heavily in the peace process, presiding over the 1993 signing of the Oslo Accords and hosting repeated rounds of negotiations between Israeli and Palestinian leaders. In 2000, he brought Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Arafat to Camp David in an effort to resolve the conflict’s most difficult issues, including borders, Israeli settlements, Palestinian refugees, security and the status of Jerusalem.

The summit ended without an agreement. Clinton continued pushing for a settlement in the final months of his presidency and later presented negotiating parameters intended to bridge the remaining gaps. Israeli and Palestinian negotiators continued discussions, but no final accord was completed before Clinton left office in January 2001.

By saying he regretted failing to persuade Arafat to accept an agreement, Clinton placed emphasis on the Palestinian leader’s decision-making at a moment when the administration believed a historic compromise was within reach. Clinton has previously argued that Arafat missed an extraordinary opportunity, though Palestinian officials and many analysts have disputed portrayals suggesting that a complete, readily acceptable agreement was simply offered and rejected.

Palestinian negotiators raised objections involving sovereignty over East Jerusalem, the territorial continuity of a future Palestinian state, control of borders and holy sites, and the rights of refugees. The precise terms evolved throughout the negotiations, and the parties never produced a mutually accepted final text.

The failure carried profound consequences. The second Palestinian uprising, or intifada, began in 2000, bringing years of bloodshed and hardening public attitudes on both sides. Subsequent American administrations attempted to revive negotiations, but the core disputes remained unresolved.

Taken together, the former presidents’ answers highlighted two distinct limits of American power. Bush commanded a dominant military coalition but stopped short of forcing a personal capitulation from Saddam. Clinton brought Israeli and Palestinian leaders closer to negotiations over final-status issues but could not secure the political decisions necessary for an agreement.

Both episodes also illustrate the difficulty of judging presidential choices in real time. Bush’s limited-war strategy protected a broad international coalition and avoided an immediate occupation of Iraq, but left Saddam in power. Clinton’s intensive diplomacy produced proposals that influenced later peace efforts, but failed to deliver the settlement he hoped would become a central part of his legacy.

Their regrets underscore a central theme of modern presidential history: battlefield victories and ambitious diplomacy can create opportunities, but they do not guarantee durable political outcomes.
